attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, summarising what he wrote earlier that day.

semantics.note: Keeps 'seemed' as 'appears' and keeps 'usage declining'. The disenchantment explanation is rightly left out. 'Seemed' softens the claim, but 'usage declining' is stated as fact, so this reads as an observation.

contract.note: Choosing September 2025 and requiring a broad usage decline is an ordinary reading of an unscoped claim. The contract fairly notes that website traffic is only a proxy. Because usage was never defined, the result depends on which measure is used.

evidence.note: Secondary summary of Lovable's web traffic falling from June to September, with an unsupported remark about other tools. Its method is unknown, it measures traffic rather than usage, and it covers one platform.
Lovable's CEO says usage grew. This is a company statement with no published series, so it is counter-context rather than an independent finding.

reviews.rationale: The only decline evidence is a secondary estimate of one platform's website traffic. The only counter-evidence is the company's own unquantified statement. Neither gives the comparable usage series across platforms that the contract requires, so the September 2025 usage claim is not settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'if and when' collapse condition and the 'in no small part' causal share. 'Large part' is a fair paraphrase.

contract.note: Requiring an industry-wide collapse before scoring, and a substantial (not sole) causal role, is a fair, ordinary reading. 'Collapse' has no threshold, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Commentary on falling AI stock prices in October 2026. It does not show an industry-wide collapse or the causal mechanism Marcus proposed.
Report of a major provider filing to go public in October 2026. This points against a collapse having already happened, but it does not prove anything about the condition sector-wide.

reviews.rationale: The condition, an industry-wide collapse of generative AI, has not been shown to have happened by the evaluation date. Under the policy, a conditional forecast whose condition is unmet or unknown is not scored. No deadline was given, so the claim stays open.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'rise and fall' and 'similar'. 'Would bet a lot of money' is high-confidence betting language, which the policy scores. The drafter's modality 'likely' understates it, but the kind (forecast) is correct.

contract.note: Reading 'rise and fall' as an adoption surge followed by a sustained decline, or permanent shutdown, is a fair, ordinary reading. The early-resolution rule matches that reading.

evidence.note: Reputable reporting that the app quickly topped Apple's App Store after launch (the rise) and that OpenAI announced it would discontinue the app.
Appfigures data show iOS monthly downloads falling from October through December 2025, while Android rose. This partly supports the decline.
OpenAI's own notice that the consumer app ended on April 26, 2026. It is a company disclosure, but it records a factual event that CBS reporting backs up. It was retrieved on the evaluation date.

reviews.rationale: The Sora app had a documented launch surge, then falling iOS downloads, then a completed permanent shutdown on April 26, 2026. That meets the contract's early-resolution rule for a rise and fall. Android growth in late 2025 does not outweigh the shutdown.
